detail: Draft states the review 'typically takes about 1 month' in time_to_first_result and calls it 'Review typically takes about 1 month after applying'. This is supported by the source ('typically in about 1 month'), so it is fine, but the summary does not note that delays are possible, which is only mentioned in risks.; Step 3 and tools_and_prompts recommend ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini for scripts, outlines and titles. The source says nothing about using AI tools for scripting. This is an unsupported add-on; it is presented as a workflow step, not as a claim from the source, but the models list and 'Prompt types' line are invented specifics.; Risk bullet 'Check YouTube's channel monetization policies before publishing content made with AI tools; you stay responsible for compliance' goes beyond the source. The source only says compliance with the monetization policies is required when you accept a partner agreement. Nothing is said about AI-made content.; Step 1 says to read the monetization policies and check country availability. Supported. Step 2 (no active Community Guidelines strikes, 2-Step Verification) is supported. The draft omits 'advanced features access on YouTube', a listed requirement, so the prerequisites are incomplete.; Step 6 'appeal within 21 days or keep uploading original content and re-apply after a waiting period' is supported, but it leaves out the 30-day and 90-day periods the source states, so it is vaguer than the source.; Step 4 thresholds are described only as 'subscribers plus public watch hours, or subscribers plus Shorts views'. The source gives exact figures (1,000 subscribers with 4,000 qualified watch hours in 12 months, or 1,000 subscribers with 10 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days). The draft is not wrong but omits them. It also drops the note that Shorts Feed watch hours do not count towards the 4,000 hours.; Step 7 states the January 31, 2027 deadline and that terms must be accepted in YouTube Studio to keep fully monetizing. Supported by the source.; Income block correctly says no income figure is stated; this is consistent with the source.; 'Difficulty: medium' and the audience line are the writer's judgment, not source claims. Acceptable, but the audience claim 'original videos or Shorts' is only loosely supported (the source mentions Shorts or long-form video and 'original content').
title: Earn ad revenue share through the YouTube Partner Program

detail: The headline claim that participants can apply to paid AI evaluation studies is inferred. The source describes 'AI training & evaluation' as a service for researchers who want domain experts in front of their models. It never says participants are offered these projects, and the sample 'Available projects' list contains none.; 'models': ['chatgpt','claude','gemini'] has no support. The source names no AI models or tools.; The step 'create a profile that describes your professional background and expertise' is not in the source. It only says participants are identity-verified and screened.; The risk 'projects can be short or one-off, so this is not a steady income' is not stated in the source. It is the writer's inference.; The AI-evaluation description ('review model answers, test for problems and give feedback') is a loose paraphrase of the researcher-facing blurb ('evaluation, red-teaming, and human feedback'). It is presented as what a participant does.; The source is a researcher-recruiting marketing page, not a participant earning guide. The dollar amounts ($150, $30, $100) appear only in an illustrative mock-up, so correctly leaving income unstated is fine, but the 'domain expert AI evaluation income' framing is weakly grounded.; Supported parts: Respondent pays participants for studies, surveys and focus groups; pay varies by project; participants are identity-verified; there is a 'Become a participant' option; screeners exist; and researchers see flags for copy-pasted or AI-written answers.
title: Get paid as a domain expert on AI evaluation studies via Respondent
